slides.text:
A variable lives at an address in memory. A pointer is a value that holds that address, so you can reach the variable without copying it.

You will take addresses, read and write through them, create variables with `new`, compare pointers and point at slice elements. Pointers in functions and structs come in the next modules.

Two operators do all the work: `&` gives the address of a variable, and `*` follows an address back to the variable.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
score = 10
p = address of score
value at p -> 10
set value at p to 25
score -> 25

notes.text: The address of score, not its value

exercises.title: Point and assign
exercises.guide: Point at the variable, then set its value through the pointer.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    lives := 3
    p := ___lives
    ___p = 5
    fmt.Println(lives)
}

exercises.title: Copy or share?
exercises.guide: Read the code and pick what it prints.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    a := 1
    b := a
    p := &a
    b = 2
    *p = 9
    fmt.Println(a, b)
}
exercises.explanation: `b := a` copies the value, so `b` is independent. `p` points at `a` itself, so `*p = 9` changes `a`.

exercises.title: A variable from new
exercises.guide: Create a variable with `new` and use it only through its pointer.

chunks.guide: `new` makes a variable of the type, set to its zero value, and returns a pointer to it.

notes.text: Allocates an int and returns its address

chunks.guide: There is no named variable here, only the pointer.

slides.text:
Copying a pointer copies the address, not the variable: both pointers reach the same place. Comparing two pointers asks whether they hold the same address, not whether the values look alike.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
a = 8, b = 8
p = address of a
q = p
r = address of b
p same address as q -> yes
p same address as r -> no
value at p equals value at r -> yes

exercises.title: Compare pointers
exercises.guide: Two pointers are equal when they hold the same address.

chunks.guide: Two variables with the same value, and three pointers. `q` is a copy of `p`.
chunks.text:
first := 8
    second := 8
    p := &first
    q := p
    r := &second

chunks.guide: Compare the addresses, then the values behind them.

notes.text: Equal only if both point at the same variable
Compares the values, not the addresses

exercises.title: Update through a pointer
exercises.guide: The assignment operators work on the pointed-at value too.

chunks.guide: Start with a counter and a pointer to it.
Increment, add and multiply through the pointer.

notes.text: Adds one to the value, not to the address

exercises.title: Adjust through a pointer
exercises.guide: Subtract 5 from the variable through the pointer, then add one.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    stock := 20
    p := &stock
    *p ___ 5
    *p ___
    fmt.Println(stock)
}

exercises.title: Swap through pointers
exercises.guide: Swap two variables using only their pointers.

chunks.guide: Two variables and a pointer to each.
Assign both values at once, so neither is lost.

notes.text: The right side is read before either side is written

exercises.title: Where does q point?
exercises.guide: Read the code and pick what it prints.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    x := 5
    y := 5
    p := &x
    q := &y
    q = p
    *q = 6
    fmt.Println(x, y, p == q)
}
exercises.explanation: `q = p` makes `q` hold the address of `x`. Writing through `q` changes `x`, `y` is untouched, and both pointers now hold the same address.
